title: ESP32-C3 hangs after about 32 VM operations while IRQs are disabled
body: I am using an ESP32-C3 with MicroPython up to commit f1bdac375240941edfc0aa04b646dc3c53d6b371. This code disables IRQs, waits approximately 1000 microseconds using ticks_us(), and then restores the returned IRQ state. Without disabling IRQs it runs, but with IRQs disabled it reaches an interrupt-watchdog timeout and restarts. I expect it to run in both cases.

symptoms_visible: On my ESP32-C3, a 1000us ticks_us() busy wait runs normally with IRQs enabled, but disabling IRQs around the same loop causes an interrupt-watchdog timeout and a restart.
N0.label: N0 IRQ-disabled wait reboot reported

symptoms_visible: My complete function saves the value returned by machine.disable_irq() and passes it to machine.enable_irq(), but it still ends in the watchdog restart.
N1_x.label: N1_x IRQ-state usage brush-off rejected

symptoms_visible: With IRQs disabled, loops containing ticks_us() calls, list operations, or even pass hang at about 32 iterations.
The same pattern occurs on ESP32-C3 and ESP32-C6, while tested ESP32 and ESP32-S2 boards continue running.
N1.label: N1 operation threshold and platform scope established

symptoms_visible: The IRQ-disabled loop does not crash on the commit immediately before 337742f6c70a7b9d407df687774bb9c9cc6a1656, and it crashes after that commit.
On the affected build, execution remains stuck until the interrupt watchdog resets the board.
N2.label: N2 regression and blocked yield localized

symptoms_visible: With my patched firmware, the IRQ-disabled loop completes instead of hanging.
The same patched firmware also keeps my webserver socket responsive instead of having it stop responding after a random period.
N3.label: N3 workaround build demonstrates scheduler interaction

symptoms_visible: On a build containing the fix, the ESP32-C3 completes the IRQ-disabled loop and restores IRQs without hanging or restarting.
N_terminal.label: terminal resolved

solution.intent: Treat the restart as incorrect use of the machine IRQ API and restore the exact state returned by machine.disable_irq().
solution.concrete_example: Save state = machine.disable_irq() and later call machine.enable_irq(state), rather than enabling IRQs without passing the saved state.

edges.comment: The initial response attributed the problem to not restoring the returned IRQ state. The reporter supplied the complete function showing that the state was already saved and restored, while the watchdog restart remained.

question_patterns: Is the failure tied to elapsed time or to a particular number of loop operations?
Can you reduce the example and find the smallest iteration count that hangs?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I reduced it further. With IRQs disabled, a list comprehension calling ticks_us(), a list comprehension containing only i, and even `for i in range(n): pass` all give the same result: at 32 or more iterations it hangs and the watchdog eventually resets the board.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The number of operations does not matter; it only resets once IRQs have been disabled continuously for the configured 300ms watchdog interval.
The boundary varies slightly between 31 and 33 iterations, but it is still operation-count based rather than elapsed-time based.

question_patterns: If you add a delay inside each iteration, does the failing iteration count change?
Does increasing the duration of each loop iteration move the approximately 32-iteration boundary?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The failing count stays around 30 to 32. Adding sleep_us(1000) inside the loop makes the reset happen after about 30ms instead of about 85us, but it still happens at the same iteration count.

question_patterns: Can this be reproduced on other ESP32 models?
Does the same test behave differently on Xtensa and RISC-V ESP32 boards?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Across our tests, the ESP32-C3 and ESP32-C6 show the problem. A genuine ESP32 and an ESP32-S2 run the same pattern without this hang.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: It reproduces identically on every tested ESP32 model, including the original ESP32 and ESP32-S2.

edges.comment: This combines the reporter's minimized reproductions with tests from other contributors, folded into one simulated user side. The raw observations establish an operation-count threshold and a RISC-V-model pattern without assigning the underlying cause. The opening report already states that the value returned by machine.disable_irq() is passed back to machine.enable_irq() and the reset still happens, so that fact is not modelled as an elicited clarification here; it enters at N0 (seed plus volunteered irq_state_returned_to_enable_irq) and only the still-open measurements gate this advance.

question_patterns: Can you reduce the function and determine whether a particular number of operations triggers the hang?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. Calling ticks_us(), building a list, or just executing `for i in range(n): pass` while IRQs are disabled hangs at 32 or more iterations.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: No operation threshold exists; it only fails after IRQs have been disabled for 300ms.

question_patterns: Does changing the time spent in each iteration change the iteration where it hangs?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: No. A tight loop can reach the failing count in about 85us, while adding sleep_us(1000) makes it take about 30ms, but the failing count remains about 30 to 32.

question_patterns: Which other ESP32 variants reproduce this?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Our ESP32-C3 and ESP32-C6 tests fail. The original ESP32 and an ESP32-S2 test work.

edges.comment: Recovery from the rejected IRQ-state suggestion. Hardware results contributed by multiple participants are folded into the simulated user side.

question_patterns: Can you test the commits immediately before and after 337742f6c70a7b9d407df687774bb9c9cc6a1656?
Is commit 337742f the change that first makes your reproducer crash?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. I tested the commit before and after 337742f6c70a7b9d407df687774bb9c9cc6a1656: before it, the test does not crash; after it, the test crashes.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Both the commit before and the commit after 337742f crash in exactly the same way.
The same first-bad commit is found using a different pair of nearby revisions.

question_patterns: Where is the affected firmware blocked when the watchdog is disabled or a debugger is attached?
Can you capture a native backtrace while it is hung?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The backtrace while it is stuck is `vPortYield()` called from `mp_thread_mutex_unlock()`, then `mp_execute_bytecode()` in py/vm.c.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The backtrace is entirely inside ticks_us() reading the hardware timer and never reaches vPortYield or the GIL code.

edges.comment: The reporter supplied the raw before/after commit result. A contributor supplied the debugger stack; both are folded into the simulated user side. Interpreting the commit and stack as a forced-yield deadlock remains engineer-side.

question_patterns: What happens if you test a build that avoids the forced context switch while IRQs are disabled?
Can you build a firmware that skips the forced context switch while IRQs are disabled and run the minimal reproducer against it?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I built and flashed my patch that checks whether IRQs are disabled before doing the forced context switch. With that firmware, the reproducer runs correctly.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: My patched firmware still hangs at 32 iterations and reaches the same watchdog reset.

edges.comment: The reporter installed and retained a custom patched firmware, so the system state changes to S2. This result validates that the hang involves the forced context switch, but it does not establish the reporter's target-specific patch as the final architectural fix. The reporter also volunteered that the patch stopped a separate intermittent webserver-socket stall and that the IRQ hang reproduced across ESP-IDF 5.0.4, 5.0.7, and 5.2.2. In the real thread the reporter had already built and volunteered this conditional-context-switch patch unprompted, so the question patterns must not presuppose that the engineer knows such a patch exists at N2.

solution.intent: Fix the ESP32 IRQ implementation so machine.disable_irq() enters a FreeRTOS-visible critical section instead of using the from-ISR interrupt-mask API, allowing the existing periodic GIL yield to remain without deadlocking RISC-V targets.
solution.concrete_example: Update the ESP32 port's machine.disable_irq()/machine.enable_irq() implementation to use the matching FreeRTOS critical-section mechanism. MicroPython had used a 'from ISR' port API to mask interrupts, so FreeRTOS did not know the interpreter was in a critical section; when the VM's periodic GIL handoff called taskYIELD() after roughly 32 branches, ESP32-C3/C6 could wait forever. Retest the minimal loop on today's build before declaring the issue resolved.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter established the approximately 32-operation threshold, the first-bad commit, the blocked vPortYield stack, and that suppressing the forced switch while IRQs are disabled avoids the hang. The maintainer inferred the precise mechanism: the ESP32 port used a 'from ISR' interrupt-mask API, so FreeRTOS did not know it was in a critical section; the fairness change in 337742f periodically released the GIL and called taskYIELD(), which can hang on the affected RISC-V path with interrupts masked. The robust fix is to repair the IRQ/critical-section contract, not merely target C3/C6 or remove GIL fairness.

edges.comment: The maintainer's candidate fix addresses the FreeRTOS contract violation exposed by commit 337742f. The reporter's conditional-yield patch was useful diagnostic evidence but was not accepted as the root-cause fix. Verification must be requested on a build containing the final change; the later memory-accounting discussion is unrelated and omitted.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the root cause: the ESP32 port masked interrupts through a FreeRTOS 'from ISR' API, leaving the kernel unaware that execution was effectively in a critical section; the periodic GIL handoff introduced by 337742f then reached taskYIELD() and could deadlock on affected RISC-V ESP32 targets.

Diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: the approximately 32-operation boundary, elapsed-time independence, ESP32-C3/C6 versus ESP32/ESP32-S2 behavior, the before/after 337742f test, and the vPortYield-from-GIL-unlock backtrace.

The final fix must use a FreeRTOS-visible critical-section mechanism for machine.disable_irq()/machine.enable_irq(), rather than merely increasing the watchdog timeout, replacing the precise loop with sleep calls, or permanently suppressing context switches only on selected chip models.
Must not settle on passing the saved IRQ state to machine.enable_irq() as the solution; the complete reproducer already does this and still resets.

The reporter's patch that skips the forced context switch while IRQs are disabled may be cited as diagnostic evidence or a temporary workaround, but it must not be presented as the preferred root-cause fix.
Must ask the reporter to retest a build containing the final fix and must not declare resolution until the IRQ-disabled loop completes without hanging or restarting.

persona_hint.experience_level: Advanced embedded MicroPython user who builds custom ESP32 firmware, changes ESP-IDF configuration, tests individual commits, writes timing-sensitive IR/RF code, and can create and flash a C-level workaround patch, but asks maintainers about scheduler and memory-management internals.
persona_hint.communication_style: Detailed, persistent, and experimental; progressively minimizes reproductions, reports exact thresholds and commit boundaries, challenges explanations that do not address the root cause, and explains the practical timing requirements of the application.
